Console API Methods.exp: The Console API provides a suite of methods for debugging directly in the browser's developer console. These tools let you log structured data, measure performance, trace execution, and group related output.Key methods include console.log() for general logging, console.table() for tabular data, console.group()/console.groupEnd() for nesting output, console.time()/console.timeEnd() for performance measurement, console.assert() for conditional logging, console.trace() for stack traces, and console.dir() for interactive object inspection.

Browser DevTools Panels.exp: Modern browser DevTools consist of specialized panels: Elements (DOM/CSS inspection), Console (JS execution), Sources (debugger with breakpoints), Network (HTTP requests), Memory (heap snapshots), Performance (profiling and flame charts), Application (storage, service workers), and Security (certificate inspection).Open DevTools with F12 or Ctrl+Shift+I. Each panel specializes in a different aspect of debugging and should be used depending on the type of issue being investigated.

Line Breakpoints.exp: Line breakpoints pause script execution at a specific line, allowing variable inspection and call stack analysis. Click the line number gutter in the Sources panel to set one. A blue arrow indicates an active breakpoint.Breakpoints survive page reloads as long as DevTools is open. They can be disabled temporarily (uncheck) or removed entirely (right-click > Remove breakpoint). Use the Breakpoints pane to manage all breakpoints at once.

Conditional Breakpoints.exp: Conditional breakpoints pause only when a condition evaluates to true. Right-click the gutter and select Add conditional breakpoint. They are shown with an orange arrow and are extremely useful for debugging specific iterations or edge cases without stopping on every call.The condition is any valid JavaScript expression. You can also use logpoints (right-click > Add logpoint) which log to the console without pausing — perfect for adding temporary logging without editing source code.

DOM & Event Breakpoints.exp: DOM Change breakpoints pause on DOM modifications: subtree modifications (children added/removed), attribute modifications (class/style), and node removal. Set them by right-clicking an element in the Elements panel.XHR/Fetch breakpoints pause when a network request matches a URL pattern. Add them in Sources > XHR/Fetch Breakpoints by clicking + and entering a URL substring.Event Listener Breakpoints pause when a specific event fires. Check event types in Sources > Event Listener Breakpoints — useful for debugging event handler chains and third-party scripts.

Exception Breakpoints & debugger.exp: Exception breakpoints pause on errors. Click the stop sign icon in Sources: once pauses on uncaught exceptions (yellow), again (blue) pauses on ALL exceptions including caught ones.The debugger; statement acts as a programmatic breakpoint. When DevTools is open, execution pauses at that line. Wrap it in conditionals for targeted debugging — but remove them before production (ESLint rule: no-debugger).

Call Stack Navigation.exp:
Call stack navigation controls are essential for stepping through code execution:
  • Step Over (F10) — execute line, stay in current function
  • Step Into (F11) — go into called functions
  • Step Out (Shift+F11) — exit current function
  • Resume (F8) — continue to next breakpoint
  • Drop Frame — rewinds to function start (restart current function execution)
The Call Stack pane shows the chain of function calls leading to the current breakpoint. Each entry is clickable — clicking it jumps to that frame and shows its scope variables.

Scope & Watch Expressions.exp: The Scope pane displays variables at each level: Local, Closure, Script, Module, Global, and Block scopes. Use it to inspect values, detect variable shadowing, and understand closure behavior.Watch Expressions evaluate JS expressions each time execution pauses. Add them in the Watch pane (Sources panel, right side below Scope) by clicking +. Examples: item.price > 50 ? 'Expensive' : 'Cheap', total.toFixed(2).Live Expressions in the Console panel (eye icon) continuously evaluate expressions in real-time, like document.title or window.innerWidth.

Async Stack Traces.exp: Async stack traces preserve the calling chain across async operations. Chrome DevTools traces promise chains, async/await calls, and setTimeout/setInterval callbacks. This is crucial for debugging asynchronous code where the traditional call stack would be lost.Understanding the event loop order is essential: synchronous code runs first, then microtasks (Promise.then, queueMicrotask), then macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval). Set breakpoints to observe execution order.

Network Panel Inspection.exp: The Network panel shows headers, payload, cookies, timing, and initiator for every request. The Initiator tab links to the source code that triggered the request. Use filters (by type, URL, status code) to isolate specific requests.Key features: Preserve log keeps requests across page reloads, Disable cache simulates first-load experience, and Throttling emulates slow network conditions (Slow 3G, Fast 3G, offline).

Storage & Application Inspection.exp: The Application panel shows all browser storage: LocalStorage, SessionStorage, Cookies, IndexedDB, Cache Storage, and more. You can view, edit, and delete entries directly — useful for debugging authentication state, cached data, and offline capabilities.For Service Workers, the Application panel allows inspecting registered workers, simulating offline mode (Offline checkbox), and triggering updates. The Clear Site Data button is handy for resetting all storage during debugging.

Memory Profiling.exp:
Memory debugging involves three key tools in DevTools:
  • Heap Snapshots — capture memory state at a point in time. Compare two snapshots to find memory leaks by filtering for Detached elements.
  • Allocation Timelines — show where memory is allocated over time. Blue bars represent new allocations, sawtooth patterns indicate garbage collection.
  • CPU Profiling — shows where execution time is spent. Record in the Performance panel. Look for long tasks (red bars > 50ms that block the main thread).
Key metrics: Shallow size (object itself) vs Retained size (object + all referenced objects).

print() & f-strings.exp: Python's print() is the simplest debugging tool. Modern f-strings (Python 3.6+) support inline variable printing with f"{var=}" syntax (Python 3.8+), format specifiers like :.2f for precision, and custom __str__/__repr__ for object representation.Use pprint for pretty-printing complex data structures. For real-time output, print to stderr with file=sys.stderr, flush=True. In production, prefer the logging module.
print() & f-strings.code:
name = "Alice"
age = 30
price = 49.99

# f-string debugging (Python 3.8+)
print(f"{name=}, {age=}, {price=:.2f}")

# Custom __repr__ for objects
class User:
    def __init__(self, id, name):
        self.id = id
        self.name = name
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"User(id={self.id}, name='{self.name}')"

user = User(1, "Alice")
print(repr(user))

# Pretty-print
import pprint
data = {"users": [{"name": "Alice", "scores": [85, 92, 78]}]}
pprint.pprint(data, indent=2)

pdb & breakpoint().exp: Python's built-in pdb module provides a full interactive debugger. The breakpoint() function (Python 3.7+) drops into the debugger at that line. IPython's ipdb offers tab completion and syntax highlighting.Key pdb commands: l (list source), n (next), s (step into), c (continue), p (print expression), pp (pretty-print), w (where/show stack), u/d (up/down stack). Set PYTHONBREAKPOINT=0 to disable all breakpoints globally.Post-mortem debugging (pdb.pm()) lets you inspect state after an exception — enter the debugger at the exact crash frame.
pdb & breakpoint().code:
def calculate_discount(price, category, is_member):
    # breakpoint() drops into pdb here
    base_discount = 0.1 if category == "electronics" else 0.05
    member_discount = 0.15 if is_member else 0.0
    total_discount = base_discount + member_discount
    final_price = price * (1 - total_discount)
    return round(final_price, 2)

breakpoint()  # Debugger stops here
result = calculate_discount(100, "electronics", True)
print(f"Result: {result}")

# Post-mortem after exception
def faulty_division(a, b):
    return a / b

try:
    faulty_division(10, 0)
except ZeroDivisionError:
    import pdb
    pdb.post_mortem()  # Inspect state at the crash point

Logging Module.exp: Python's logging module provides hierarchical loggers, multiple handlers (Stream, File, Rotating, Syslog, SMTP), formatters, and configurable levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL).Configure via basicConfig() or dictConfig. Loggers follow a hierarchy — child loggers propagate to parents. Debug logger setup by inspecting logger.handlers, logger.getEffectiveLevel(), and logger.propagate.Use third-party logger level control: logging.getLogger("urllib3").setLevel(logging.WARNING) to suppress verbose libraries.
Logging Module.code:
import logging
import sys

# Basic configuration
logging.basicConfig(
    level=logging.DEBUG,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(name)s: %(message)s",
    stream=sys.stdout,
)

# Logger hierarchy
parent = logging.getLogger("app")
child = logging.getLogger("app.service")

parent.setLevel(logging.WARNING)
child.setLevel(logging.DEBUG)

parent.debug("Filtered - won't show")
child.debug("Shows via child logger")

# Debug logger setup
print(f"Effective level: {child.getEffectiveLevel()}")
print(f"Handlers: {logging.getLogger().handlers}")
print(f"Propagate: {child.propagate}")

Exception Hooks & Tracebacks.exp: Python's exception handling uses try/except/else/finally blocks. The sys.excepthook intercepts uncaught exceptions globally for logging. The traceback module provides utilities for extracting, formatting, and printing stack traces.The inspect module gives deeper introspection: inspect.stack() shows call frames, inspect.getsource() retrieves source code, and inspect.signature() shows function parameters. Use gc.get_referrers() to find what holds references to objects.
Exception Hooks & Tracebacks.code:
import sys
import traceback
import inspect

# Custom exception hook
def global_handler(exc_type, exc_value, exc_traceback):
    print(f"=== {exc_type.__name__}: {exc_value} ===")
    traceback.print_tb(exc_traceback)

sys.excepthook = global_handler

# Stack inspection
def deep_func():
    frame = inspect.currentframe()
    for i, finfo in enumerate(inspect.stack()):
        print(f"[{i}] {finfo.function} at {finfo.filename}:{finfo.lineno}")

def middle():
    deep_func()

middle()

# Reference tracking
import gc
obj = [1, 2, 3]
print(f"Referrers: {len(gc.get_referrers(obj))}")

IDE & Remote Debugging.exp: Modern IDEs provide visual debugging for Python. VS Code and PyCharm offer breakpoints, variable inspection, watch expressions, and step-through controls.For remote debugging, use debugpy: call debugpy.listen() to start the debug server, then attach from your IDE. For testing, use pytest --pdb to enter the debugger on test failure. Jupyter supports %debug for post-mortem inspection after errors.
IDE & Remote Debugging.code:
# VS Code launch.json for Python:
# {
#     "version": "0.2.0",
#     "configurations": [{
#         "name": "Python: Current File",
#         "type": "python",
#         "request": "launch",
#         "program": "${file}",
#         "console": "integratedTerminal",
#         "justMyCode": true
#     }]
# }

def fibonacci(n):
    if n <= 0: return []
    elif n == 1: return [0]
    elif n == 2: return [0, 1]
    seq = [0, 1]
    for i in range(2, n):
        seq.append(seq[i-1] + seq[i-2])
    return seq

# Remote debugging with debugpy
# import debugpy
# debugpy.listen(("0.0.0.0", 5678))
# debugpy.wait_for_client()

result = fibonacci(10)
print("Fibonacci:", result)
print("Use pytest --pdb -x to debug test failures")

Source Maps.exp: Source maps map compiled JavaScript back to original TypeScript source code. Enable with sourceMap: true in tsconfig.json. Chrome DevTools automatically loads .map files to show TS code in the Sources panel.For production, upload source maps to error tracking services (Sentry, Bugsnag, Datadog) so stack traces point back to original source. Use sentry-cli, datadog-ci, or bugsnag-sourcemaps for upload. Always strip source maps from production static assets to avoid exposing source code.

Workspace Overrides & Pretty-Printing.exp: Workspace Overrides let you edit files directly in Sources and persist changes across page reloads. Enable in Sources > Filesystem > Add folder to workspace. Edits are saved to a local folder and take effect on every reload — no server changes needed.Pretty-printing ({ } button in Sources panel) reformats minified code into readable JS. The Blackbox feature hides framework/lib scripts from stack traces. Use //# sourceURL=name.js for naming eval'd code in the Sources panel.

REPL & Node.js Remote Debugging.exp: Node.js debugging with --inspect flags enables Chrome DevTools connection. Use --inspect-brk to pause on first line. Connect via chrome://inspect and click "Open dedicated DevTools for Node".The Node.js REPL provides an interactive debugging environment with commands: .help, .break (exit multi-line), .save (save session), .load (load file), .editor (multi-line editing). The repl module lets you create custom REPLs with defined commands.

Memory Leak Patterns.exp:
Memory leaks occur when objects are retained unintentionally. Common patterns:
  • Uncleared intervals/timers — always save the interval ID and clear on unmount
  • Detached DOM references — removing elements from DOM but keeping JS references
  • Accidental globals — undeclared variables (x = 5 without let/const)
  • Closures retaining large data — closures capture the entire outer scope
  • Forgotten event listeners — listeners on removed elements prevent GC
Use Chrome DevTools Memory panel > Heap snapshots to identify leaks. Compare two snapshots and filter by "Detached" to find retained DOM elements.

Error Tracking & Monitoring.exp: Production error tracking tools (Sentry, LogRocket, Datadog RUM) capture errors with context: browser, device, user actions, and network state. Integrate via SDK for real-time monitoring with source map support.Set up global error handlers: window.onerror for runtime errors and unhandledrejection for promise rejections. These provide a safety net for errors that slip through try/catch blocks.

Network Mocking & Blocking.exp: The Network panel in DevTools supports request blocking, mocking, and offline simulation. Right-click a request > Block request URL to simulate API failures. Use the Network conditions panel to emulate offline mode, custom latency, and specific user agents.For browser extensions debugging, use chrome://extensions (Chrome) or about:debugging (Firefox). Enable developer mode to inspect background scripts, content scripts, and popup pages. Manifest V3 extensions use Service Workers — inspect them in Application > Service Workers.

Go Debugging.exp: Delve is the standard debugger for Go programs. Key commands: break (set breakpoint), continue (resume), next (step over), step (step into), print (evaluate expression), goroutines (list all goroutines).Go's built-in race detector (go run -race) finds concurrent access bugs. The pprof tool provides CPU, heap, goroutine, and block profiling via net/http/pprof. Use go tool trace for execution trace visualization.
